title: Practical ABAP design patterns and trade-offs
intro: Use patterns to explain a concrete design decision, not to recite a catalog. These original senior scenarios build on OO-09 through OO-12 and distinguish pattern mechanics from RAP transaction, API-release and security contracts. SAP's pattern examples are exploratory demonstrations, not production templates. Verify syntax and dependencies on the target release. Recommendations below are contextual analysis, not claims that SAP mandates a particular application architecture.

questions.question: Approval rules vary by country, while the application workflow should remain stable. Strategy or Template Method?
questions.answer: Prefer an injected Strategy when approval calculation is the variation and the caller should select or replace it without changing its own class hierarchy. Template Method fits a deliberately stable algorithm skeleton with controlled subclass extension steps. Here, I would keep workflow coordination separate from country rules and pass explicit context to the selected rule. Inheritance becomes justified only if its protected extension contract and lifecycle are genuinely stable requirements.
questions.detail: A country rule should return a decision rather than commit, send email or modify hidden global state. Test the same coordinator with several rule implementations. If countries also vary the process sequence, revisit the workflow model instead of adding increasingly powerful hooks that subclasses can use to violate invariants.
questions.pitfall: Choosing inheritance solely to share code, or allowing a rule implementation to take over transaction ownership.
followups: Which variation changes at runtime rather than through subclassing?
How would you prevent a new rule from changing the workflow's transaction boundary?
signals: Separates algorithm variation from coordination
Defends composition versus inheritance contextually
Keeps rules substitutable and independently testable
questions.evidence: Run identical coordinator contract tests with two country rules and a test double; assert decision and side-effect boundaries.

questions.question: A posting integration needs matching serializer and sender implementations for each provider. Is one static factory sufficient?
questions.answer: A simple factory can centralize selection for a small fixed set of implementations. Abstract Factory becomes useful when callers must obtain a compatible family, such as a provider-specific serializer and sender, without mixing families. Factory Method instead delegates creation through a subclass-overridable creation operation. I would choose the smallest construction design that protects the actual compatibility rule, rather than calling every method returning an object the Factory Method pattern.
questions.detail: For two stable providers, an explicit factory returning a validated pair may suffice. If multiple related products evolve independently, a provider-factory interface can make their compatibility visible. Fail clearly for unknown configuration and test family consistency; silently selecting a default provider can post to the wrong destination.
questions.pitfall: Confusing a static creation helper with inheritance-based Factory Method or introducing an Abstract Factory for one trivial object.
followups: What concrete invalid combination must construction prevent?
When would adding a creator subclass be better than changing a configuration map?
signals: Distinguishes three creation approaches
Names a real product-family invariant
Includes invalid configuration and evolution costs
questions.evidence: Test each supported provider family and an unknown provider; verify no serializer/sender cross-pairing can be constructed.

questions.question: A legacy posting API has awkward parameters and a three-step prepare/check/post sequence. Would you build an Adapter, a Facade, or both?
questions.answer: Use an Adapter to translate the application's posting contract into the legacy API's types, identities and error representation. A Facade can expose a coherent business operation over the three underlying steps. They may coexist, but their boundaries must preserve authorization, failure information and transaction ownership. Neither pattern makes an unreleased API eligible for ABAP Cloud use or removes a nested commit. I would reject a superficially clean wrapper that hides those constraints.
questions.detail: Separate mapping tests from orchestration tests. For example, verify that a zero amount remains explicit, API warnings do not become unconditional success, and a failed check prevents posting. Expose an uncertain remote outcome distinctly from a definitive rejection so callers can reconcile instead of duplicating work.
questions.pitfall: Treating any wrapper as both a supported API and a transaction adapter without inspecting its dependencies.
followups: Which errors belong to the domain contract and which retain technical detail?
What evidence would make the legacy API unsuitable despite a neat interface?
signals: Separates contract translation from subsystem orchestration
Preserves transactional and release constraints
Tests meaningful error and value mapping
questions.evidence: Trace all three steps with injected failures and inspect dependency release state; assert no hidden commit or swallowed business rejection.

questions.question: You want timing, diagnostic logging and retries around an outbound service. Would stacked Decorators be safe?
questions.answer: Decorators can add behavior around the same service interface without creating subclasses for every combination. I would make order explicit and preserve the wrapped contract, especially exceptions, authorization context and return values. Retrying is not a harmless decoration: it requires operation-specific idempotency and classification of uncertain outcomes. I would enable retries only where the service contract supports them, and decide whether timing and logging describe each attempt or the overall logical operation.
questions.detail: A logging decorator outside a retry decorator records one logical call; inside it, it can observe individual attempts. Both can be useful if correlated clearly. Redact sensitive payloads and ensure diagnostic failure does not silently change a successful business result unless the required audit contract explicitly demands that behavior.
questions.pitfall: Adding automatic retries to every POST or assuming decorator order cannot change observable behavior.
followups: Which wrapper should count attempts and which should measure total latency?
How does a timeout after remote success affect the retry policy?
signals: Preserves the component interface contract
Reasons about wrapper ordering
Separates retries from idempotency guarantees
questions.evidence: Test wrapper orders, a transient read failure, uncertain write completion and logging failure; inspect returned outcome and number of remote effects.

questions.question: Three handlers can route a request to an approver. The first matching rule should win. How would you implement and test Chain of Responsibility?
questions.answer: Model the decision contract explicitly: handled, not applicable and failed are different outcomes. An ordered Chain of Responsibility fits first-match routing when each handler can accept the request or pass it onward. Validate configuration order and define the no-match outcome. If the business instead needs every validation result, use an explicit validation pipeline or collection rather than stopping at the first successful handler and assuming the rest of the checks ran.
questions.detail: Put the most specific route ahead of a general fallback only when that precedence is intended. Avoid hidden database writes in a routing handler; return a decision that the transaction coordinator applies. Log the rule identity so support can explain why the request reached a particular approver.
questions.pitfall: Treating an exception as 'not applicable', or confusing first-match routing with execute-all validation.
followups: What happens when two handlers match?
How is a configuration error different from a valid request with no applicable route?
signals: Defines routing outcomes and precedence
Distinguishes chain from validation pipeline
Keeps decisions explainable and side effects controlled
questions.evidence: Test overlapping rules, no match, handler failure and reordered configuration; assert exactly which handlers execute and which route is chosen.

questions.question: A local ABAP event updates an ALV, and the team proposes another handler to start an external workflow. What boundary has changed?
questions.answer: The local Observer arrangement is suitable for notifying listeners in the current execution context. Starting a durable external workflow introduces commit, delivery, retry and recovery requirements that an ordinary ABAP Objects event does not supply. I would keep local display notification separate from a committed business transition and use an appropriate transactional publication mechanism for the integration. Multiple listeners also require an explicit policy for exceptions and lifecycle registration.
questions.detail: Registering multiple listener instances, failing to deregister obsolete listeners, or retaining state across tests can produce surprising local notifications. For the workflow, duplicate delivery and delayed events require durable consumer correlation and state checks. Do not infer asynchronous durability merely because the publisher does not directly name the receiving class.
questions.pitfall: Assuming SET HANDLER creates a durable subscription or that Observer guarantees exactly-once business effects.
followups: Which part of the design survives an application-server restart?
What if one local listener fails after another already changed its state?
signals: Distinguishes in-process notification from durable messaging
Coordinates external effects with committed state
Defines listener and consumer failure handling
questions.evidence: Test local listener registration separately from rejected save, duplicate event and delayed workflow delivery cases.

questions.question: A command object represents Submit and can be queued or retried. Does using Command make execution idempotent or undoable?
questions.answer: No. Command packages an operation and its inputs; durability, authorization, idempotency and compensation are additional contracts. I would assign a stable business operation identity, decide how it is stored with the state transition, and define responses to repeated execution or conflicting payload reuse. An undo method is only meaningful where a valid inverse exists. A posted document may require a compensating business operation rather than deletion or an in-memory rollback.
questions.detail: A command held only in memory is not a reliable job queue. When persistence is required, store a versioned data contract and reconstruct an eligible executor; do not treat an arbitrary object reference as a durable payload. Recheck the relevant authorization and business state at execution time.
questions.pitfall: Assuming execute can safely run twice or that every business command has an exact inverse.
followups: What result should a retry return after the first response was lost?
How would you evolve a persisted command payload across application releases?
signals: Separates encapsulation from execution guarantees
Defines durable identity and replay behavior
Uses compensation where reversal is not exact
questions.evidence: Simulate duplicate execution, conflicting payload reuse, lost response and executor upgrade; assert one effective transition and traceable recovery.

questions.question: A repository interface improves testability, but its RAP implementation reads managed persistence directly. What can go wrong?
questions.answer: The seam may be useful while the implementation is transactionally incorrect. A direct table read can miss creates, updates and deletes still in the RAP buffer. Define whether the repository contract means persisted state or the current transactional view; for transaction-sensitive BO logic, use the appropriate EML behavior access. Do not add a generic repository that writes managed tables and bypasses RAP checks. Test doubles must reproduce the relevant contract, not merely return convenient rows.
questions.detail: A reporting query and a validation inside a modify flow can legitimately need different read semantics. Give those contracts distinct names or responsibilities. Test an update followed by a read before save, plus create and delete cases; an isolated unit test alone will not reveal a wrong persistence shortcut.
questions.pitfall: Equating a mockable interface with correct behavior or recreating RAP's transactional buffer in a second general-purpose cache.
followups: Which caller actually needs persisted rather than buffered state?
What integration test would fail if the repository used SELECT instead of EML?
signals: Defines explicit read semantics
Respects RAP ownership and buffer visibility
Combines seam tests with real integration evidence
questions.evidence: Compare unsaved create/update/delete reads through the adapter with the BO contract, then run rollback and save paths on the target system.

questions.question: A singleton caches the current approver and makes tests pass alone but fail as a suite. How do you redesign its lifetime?
questions.answer: I would remove request-specific mutable state from the singleton and make dependencies explicit. A conventional ABAP singleton is scoped to its internal session, not to all users or the whole landscape, and its lifetime can exceed one test or business operation. Prefer a freshly constructed, context-aware service or a cache with explicit key, scope and invalidation. If a shared instance is justified, specify immutability or cleanup rules and provide deterministic substitution in tests.
questions.detail: Caching the 'current user' implicitly is particularly dangerous for reusable jobs or delegated processing. Passing business context into the operation makes the dependency visible. A reset method can stabilize legacy tests temporarily, but it does not repair a production lifetime that is inconsistent with the data being cached.
questions.pitfall: Claiming singleton means one system-wide instance or solving hidden state solely by forcing test order.
followups: What exact lifetime is required by the cached value?
How would two simulated users in one test expose the defect?
signals: Scopes singleton state accurately
Removes hidden request context
Distinguishes test cleanup from production correctness
questions.evidence: Run tests in multiple orders and reuse one session across different users or contexts; assert no stale decisions and deterministic dependency replacement.

questions.question: A service obtains every dependency from a global factory inside its methods. How would you introduce dependency injection without building a framework?
questions.answer: At a composition root near the application boundary, construct the service with its required interface-typed dependencies. Keep wiring separate from business decisions so tests can provide controlled collaborators and new dependencies are visible. A factory can help build a complicated dependency graph, but repeated global lookup inside domain methods hides that graph. Start with straightforward constructor injection for required services; do not introduce a container when explicit construction remains readable.
questions.detail: Framework-owned classes may constrain construction, so create a small delegated application service or use a supported seam instead of inventing framework constructor parameters. Ensure test setup cannot accidentally fall back to a live posting client. Use integration tests to verify production wiring separately from pure decision tests.
questions.pitfall: Replacing one hidden global singleton with a service locator and calling the result fully decoupled.
followups: Which object owns construction in a framework-created RAP handler?
How would a newly added dependency become visible to existing tests?
signals: Separates composition from domain logic
Uses explicit dependencies with framework awareness
Verifies production wiring and safe test substitution
questions.evidence: Instantiate the application service with doubles, assert no live dependency access, and test the production factory's intended object graph independently.

questions.question: A small report has one stable calculation. A reviewer requests Strategy, Abstract Factory and Repository 'for clean architecture'. How do you respond?
questions.answer: I would ask which real variation, dependency boundary or testing obstacle each abstraction resolves. A small named method with explicit inputs can be the better current design. Add a seam where an external dependency obstructs meaningful tests, and introduce polymorphism when distinct behaviors actually need independent evolution. Pattern count is not a quality metric. I would preserve readability and leave a concrete refactoring trigger instead of building speculative extension layers.
questions.detail: For example, a pure tax-base calculation with one supported rule can remain a function-like method with boundary tests. A remote rate source may deserve an interface now because it fails independently. If a second rule later appears, extract a Strategy without pretending the initial absence of one was a design defect.
questions.pitfall: Equating more classes with greater maintainability or rejecting all patterns because the current implementation is short.
followups: Which expected change would justify the next abstraction?
What testing benefit can you demonstrate before adding another interface?
signals: Connects abstraction to a concrete force
Balances simplicity with testable external boundaries
Defines an observable refactoring trigger
questions.evidence: Compare change scope and tests for the current design and proposed abstraction; retain only boundaries with a demonstrated maintenance or testing benefit.

questions.question: A factory selects country approval Strategies from configuration. How do you keep that combination safe, explainable and testable?
questions.answer: Use a small explicit mapping from supported configuration values to eligible Strategy implementations, then inject the selected strategy into the coordinator. Validate missing and unsupported configuration instead of silently defaulting to a permissive rule. Keep strategy selection separate from its business decision and preserve a common result contract. If dynamic construction is used, it still needs controlled class selection and release-compatible dependencies; it is not a way around ABAP Cloud API restrictions.
questions.detail: Record which policy version produced the decision when business audit requires it. Test selection independently from each rule and run a common contract suite across strategies. Configuration changes must not make an in-flight approval unpredictably switch policy; decide whether it uses current policy or a recorded policy version.
questions.pitfall: Allowing arbitrary class names from untrusted input or implementing a 'default approve' path when configuration lookup fails.
followups: What should happen to a pending request after the configured policy changes?
Which tests distinguish factory-selection failure from a correct rule rejecting the request?
signals: Separates selection and execution
Fails safely on configuration errors
Defines versioned policy and common contracts
questions.evidence: Test supported and unknown countries, policy changes during pending approvals and identical contract assertions against every Strategy.
